##### **1. Introduction**  
The Brazilian pre-salt is a domain in ultra-deep ocean water that holds giant oil and gas accumulations, but remains a production challenge due to its diverse depositional and diagenetic history (Bruhn et al., 2017). This domain extends through the Santos and Campos Basins, comprising carbonate rocks that were originally deposited as sediments under a lacustrine environment during the Aptian age. These rocks were formed in a rift-sag stage context and are overlain by a thick  
layer of evaporites. Numerous models have been proposed to characterize the pre-salt reservoirs, coupling their complex evolutionary history with several studies on their unusual depositional features, diagenetic outcomes, and reservoir quality (Gomes et al., 2020; Pietzsch et al., 2020; Wright and Barnett, 2015).

They developed in the context of the opening of the South Atlantic, which resulted in numerous horsts (structural highs) and grabens (structural lows) (Pietzsch et al., 2018). Ostracods can live in environments deeper and more saline than mollusks, and they can become abundant in those stressed environments (Fl¨ugel, 1982; Scholle and Ulmer-Scholle, 2003). Hence, ostracods in the absence of mollusks suggest an environment either relatively deep or very saline. Ostracods are small, so even gentle currents can move them and winnow out muds, forming ostracod grainstones. Ostracod wackestones and packstones could have accumulated in deeper, low-energy environments. The absence of mollusks and ostracods in dolomitic mudstones suggests times when the upper synrift lakes became too saline for mollusks and ostracods. Ooid grainstones probably accumulated in lacustrine environments with continual or repeated agitation, similar to some windward coastlines in the modern Great Salt Lake (Eardley, 1938).

The Intraclastic Grainstones (F3) are composed of fragments of calcite spherulites, shrubs or both. The fragments are characterized by very angular to well-rounded shapes, with dimensions varying from 0.3 to less to 5 mm (Fig. 4a, b). Cementation and replacement by dolomite (rhombic euhedral–subhedral or mosaic texture), megaquartz (euhedral or mosaic), microquartz and, rarely, calcite makes it hard to visualize the intraclasts limits locally (Fig. 4c, d). Rift basins typically comprise three main tectono- stratigraphic stages; pre- , syn- and post- rift. The syn- rift stage is often characterised by the deposition of asymmetric wedges of growth strata that record differential subsidence caused by active normal faulting. The subsequent post- rift stage is defined by longwavelength subsidence driven by lithospheric cooling and is typified by the deposition of broadly tabular stratal packages that drape any rift- related relief. The stratigraphic contact between syn- and post- rift rocks is often thought to be represented by an erosional unconformity. However, the late syn- rift to early postrift stratigraphic record is commonly far more complex since (i) the associated tectonic transition is not instantaneous; (ii) net subsidence may be punctuated by transient periods of uplift; and (iii) strain often migrates oceanward during rifting until continental breakup is achieved with crustal rupture

The studied Aptian carbonates of the Santos basin constitute a 100-m-thick stratigraphic sequence that corresponds to part of the upper portion of the Barra Velha Formation, Guaratiba Group, whose sediments were deposited during the sag phase of the basin (Fig. 2).

#### **2. Location and geological framework**  
The Santos Basin (Fig. 1) is a passive margin basin related to the Gondwana breakup event during the Neocominian. The tectonic evolution of this basin is divided into three mega-sequences: rift, post-rift (sag), and drift presented in Fig. 2 (Mio et al., 2005; Moreira et al., 2007). The Camboriú, Piçarras, and Itapema formations represent the rift stage, related to the separation of South-American and African paleocontinents during the end of Neocomian and the beginning of Aptian and are responsible for initiating the lacustrine deposition (Moreira et al., 2007).  
The post-rift or sag sequence represents a transitional stage from continental to marine environment with softer tectonics during the Aptian (Moreira et al., 2007). This transitional stage is represented by the non-marine and shallow-water carbonates of the Barra Velha Formation and the thick overlying evaporite seal of the Ariri Formation (Buckley et al., 2015).

#### Spherulitestone (F1)  
This facies is composed primarily of spherulites and secondarily of hybrid forms. The spherulites consist of spherical to elliptical calcite (or aragonite) aggregates of crystals with a fibro-radial structure (Chafetz et al. 2018) (Fig. 2a). Their shape varies from very regular and rounded edges to somewhat rough edges. They also show a typical radial extinction in polarized light. Rift basins typically comprise three main tectono- stratigraphic stages; pre- , syn- and post- rift. The syn- rift stage is often characterised by the deposition of asymmetric wedges of growth strata that record differential subsidence caused by active normal faulting. The subsequent post- rift stage is defined by longwavelength subsidence driven by lithospheric cooling and is typified by the deposition of broadly tabular stratal packages that drape any rift- related relief. The stratigraphic contact between syn- and post- rift rocks is often thought to be represented by an erosional unconformity. However, the late syn- rift to early postrift stratigraphic record is commonly far more complex since (i) the associated tectonic transition is not instantaneous; (ii) net subsidence may be punctuated by transient periods of uplift; and (iii) strain often migrates oceanward during rifting until continental breakup is achieved with crustal rupture

Firstly, it is important to comprehend some tectonostratigraphic models, particularly the ones presented in Bosence (1998). This model describes the term syn-rift as a  
period of basin evolution characterized by mechanical extension. It is also reflected in stratigraphic features that indicate syn-depositional fault movement. The post-rift term denotes any strata that form after the active extensional tectonics.

Spherulitic shrubstones are in-situ facies with more than 50% of shrubs, spherulites, and less than 10% of mud (Gomes et al., 2020). These facies typically have medium (0,5 to 1,5 cm) to coarse shrubs ( _>_ 1, 5 cm) and very fine to coarse spherulites that occur either on the top or between the shrub branches (Fig. 6A and B). Several intermediate grain forms between spherulites and shrubs are found in these facies, resulting in oval grains, as shown in Fig. 6B. Fining-upward pattern commonly occurs, with medium (0,5 to 1,5 cm) to coarse ( _>_ 1,5 cm) shrubs grading to smaller shrubs (0,2–0,5 cm), or spherulites.  
These facies rarely preserve evidence of the original rock matrix. Cementation by calcite, dolomite, and silica is common. Fabric selective porosity is the most common. It is characterized by large porous spaces between the shrub branches, intra-shrub porosity due to grain dissolution is also common.

Spherulitic shrubstones with mud are in situ facies with a predominance of shrubs ( _>_ 50%), occurrence of spherulites, and more than 10% of mud (Gomes et al., 2020). These facies commonly form thin layers that occur intercalated with Shrubby spherulitestones with mud, forming diffuse and gradual contacts hardly distinguishable on a macroscopic scale (Fig. 8A).

#### **6. Conclusions**  
In this study, we have characterized the Búzios Field in three dimensions using 3D seismic data, seismic attributes, and well-log data. The combined use of these tools enabled the understanding of important parameters within the tectonostratigraphic evolution of the Santos Basin. Specifically, we examined how the relative position of the study area concerning the continental margin influences the amount of displacement observed in the region and how this positioning affects the mobilization and thickness of the salt package.

Rift basins typically comprise three main tectono- stratigraphic stages; pre- , syn- and post- rift. The syn- rift stage is often characterised by the deposition of asymmetric wedges of growth strata that record differential subsidence caused by active normal faulting. The subsequent post- rift stage is defined by longwavelength subsidence driven by lithospheric cooling and is typified by the deposition of broadly tabular stratal packages that drape any rift- related relief. The stratigraphic contact between syn- and post- rift rocks is often thought to be represented by an erosional unconformity. Rift basins typically comprise three main tectono- stratigraphic stages; pre- , syn- and post- rift. The syn- rift stage is often characterised by the deposition of asymmetric wedges of growth strata that record differential subsidence caused by active normal faulting. The subsequent post- rift stage is defined by longwavelength subsidence driven by lithospheric cooling and is typified by the deposition of broadly tabular stratal packages that drape any rift- related relief. The stratigraphic contact between syn- and post- rift rocks is often thought to be represented by an erosional unconformity. However, the late syn- rift to early postrift stratigraphic record is commonly far more complex since (i) the associated tectonic transition is not instantaneous; (ii) net subsidence may be punctuated by transient periods of uplift; and (iii) strain often migrates oceanward during rifting until continental breakup is achieved with crustal rupture

Classical models of rift basin evolution are based on the analysis of the sedimentary record preserved within individual grabens and half- grabens; studies such as these typically allow the timing and duration of these stages to be constrained (e.g. Bosence, 1998; Gawthorpe & Leeder, 2000; Prosser, 1993). In these models, the syn- rift stage is characterised by mechanical subsidence, marked by the generation of large amounts of accommodation over a relatively short period. Mechanical subsidence occurs due to movement/slip along normal faults and the associated rotation of fault blocks, resulting in differential subsidence and the formation of grabens or half- grabens, separated by horsts (i.e. basement highs)

#### Finely Laminated Mudstone  
This is a finely laminated micritic mudstone associated with discontinuous laminations of silica (chert). Scattered euhedral crystalline crystals of dolomite occur in a brown-colored matrix, containing clays with preserved organic matter (kerogen). This interpretation signals that these facies occur on basal part of the cycles, which may represent a flooding event during increase of lake level (Figure 12E).  
#### Massive Mudstone  
This is composed of pure and normally dolomitized facies with porosity of up to 19% and permeability that can reach 3350 mD. It contains rare closed, articulated shells of ostracods, pyrite crystals, and secondary euhedral quartz. Thick successions of massive mudstone are found in the uppermost part of the presalt sequence, being one of the best reservoirs in terms of porosity. Massive micrite facies can be suggestive of micrite precipitation of carbonate in low-energy environments (Tucker and Wright, 1990; Figure 12F).

**From Plug to Reservoir: An Integrated Multiscale Approach.** The multiscale approach adopted in this study, with petrophysical characterization related to reservoir pore types, allows for a more accurate evaluation of pore distribution and connectivity throughout the reservoir. Porosity values derived from CT were analyzed along the core profile. In general, CT porosity tends to be underestimated due to resolution limits, with segmentation performed only for macropores. NLD: Intrusive igneous rock is an igneous rock that forms when magma is emplaced within pre-existing strata and crystallizes below the surface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Mero/Libra area, these bodies are mainly Santonian/Campanian alkaline intrusions that may cut surrounding rocks or occur concordant with sedimentary layering, including near the top of the Barra Velha Formation. They are critical to reservoir characterization because they reduce effective reservoir volume, may act as flow barriers or fractured high-permeability intervals, and can induce hydrothermal alteration that commonly tightens adjacent carbonates.

Until now, two main producing trends have been established in the Santos Basin.  
- The first, a postsalt trend, was discovered during the initial exploration in the shallow waters (<400 m) parallel to the coastline, where Upper Cretaceous Coniacian-, Santonian-, Campanian-, and possibly the Maastrichtian-Age turbiditic sands and Albian oolitic limestone were initially established as gas and oil/condensate-prone reservoirs (Figure 1). The Santos Basin (Fig. 1) is a passive margin basin related to the Gondwana breakup event during the Neocominian. The tectonic evolution of this basin is divided into three mega-sequences: rift, post-rift (sag), and drift presented in Fig. 2 (Mio et al., 2005; Moreira et al., 2007). The Camboriú, Piçarras, and Itapema formations represent the rift stage, related to the separation of South-American and African paleocontinents during the end of Neocomian and the beginning of Aptian and are responsible for initiating the lacustrine deposition (Moreira et al., 2007).  
The post-rift or sag sequence represents a transitional stage from continental to marine environment with softer tectonics during the Aptian (Moreira et al., 2007). This transitional stage is represented by the non-marine and shallow-water carbonates of the Barra Velha Formation and the thick overlying evaporite seal of the Ariri Formation (Buckley et al., 2015).
